title: How should a personal assistant brief a household chef?
body_markdown:
A personal assistant should brief a household chef with a written record of who is eating, dietary requirements, meal preferences, cooking dates, kitchen arrangements and approval responsibilities. Keep standing instructions separate from weekly changes. Confirm groceries, equipment, clearing up and spending authorisation before the first visit; do not treat an enquiry as an agreed booking.


**TL;DR**

- A personal assistant household chef brief should separate standing household instructions from weekly meal planning.
- Record allergies separately from preferences, and ask the chef to confirm whether the requirements can be accommodated.
- Give one named contact responsibility for menu approval, household changes and spending authorisation.
- myCHEF provides vetted chefs for household cooking and weekly meal prep in Dubai.


## How should a personal assistant brief a household chef?

**Send one approved household brief, then use a short update for each cooking visit.** The household brief explains how the kitchen and household operate. The visit update confirms what has changed: diners, meals, ingredients, access or timing.

If you are still deciding how recurring cooking should fit around the household, the guide to [monthly private chef arrangements](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/can-i-book-a-private-chef-in-dubai-on-a-monthly-basis) addresses that next question. This article focuses on the instructions a personal assistant should prepare, rather than choosing a booking plan.

Build the initial brief in this order:

1. **Define the service.** State whether you need meals cooked for immediate eating, weekly meal preparation, or a combination to discuss.
2. **Identify the diners.** Separate adults, children, household staff and occasional guests where their meals differ.
3. **Record dietary requirements.** Distinguish allergies, intolerances, religious requirements and preferences.
4. **Describe the kitchen.** Include equipment, storage, access and any restrictions on use.
5. **Assign decisions.** Name who approves menus, ingredient substitutions, purchases and schedule changes.
6. **Confirm the handover.** Agree how finished meals, storage instructions and unresolved questions will be communicated.

Ask the chef or service coordinator to acknowledge the brief and identify anything that needs clarification. Sending instructions is not the same as receiving confirmation.

## Why separate household instructions from weekly updates?

A standing brief should not need rewriting whenever the family has an extra lunch at home. Equally, a permanent food restriction should not disappear inside a message about tomorrow’s arrival time.

Use two clearly named records: **Household brief** and **Visit update**. These are suggested working documents, not a requirement to use particular software.

| Record | Best for | What belongs here | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Household brief | Stable instructions | Dietary requirements, kitchen equipment, access process, approval contacts | Becomes unreliable if changes are not recorded |
| Visit update | The next cooking session | Diners, meals, menu approval, ingredients already at home | Cannot replace the standing dietary record |

Keep the approved version accessible to the people who need it. If you use a shared document, identify who can edit it; if you send messages, clearly mark which version replaces the previous instructions.

Do not circulate the entire household schedule just to explain a kitchen visit. Share the access and timing information needed for the cooking assignment, and handle sensitive access details through the household’s agreed channel.


![Standing household instructions separated from the details that change for each cooking visit](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/34ca46a1-5eba-4bbd-996a-da56b45dafc0/body-be163d5a3bb1f35e5aa14d24d9c5492f.jpg)

*Keep permanent instructions separate from the details of the next visit.*


## What information belongs in the household brief?

### Who is eating, and what meals are needed?

Specify which meals the chef is being asked to prepare. “Family meals” does not explain whether you mean breakfast preparation, packed lunches, dinner or food for later use.

Record portions by diner group where useful, without assuming children and adults want the same dishes. Describe appetite and preferred serving style in ordinary language. Ask the chef to propose quantities rather than supplying an unsupported universal portion rule.

If guests are expected, identify whether they are joining normal household meals or attending a separate occasion. A birthday dinner or celebration needs its own private dining or catering brief, even when it takes place in the same kitchen.

### Which dietary instructions are non-negotiable?

Give allergies and intolerances their own clearly marked field. Do not combine them with dislikes such as avoiding mushrooms or preferring mild seasoning.

For each requirement, identify the affected diner and the relevant ingredients or restrictions. Ask the chef to confirm what can be accommodated in the household kitchen, including any concerns about shared equipment or ingredient substitutions.

Record religious food requirements explicitly. Do not assume that a cuisine name explains every ingredient or preparation requirement. If instructions come from a healthcare professional, pass on the approved guidance rather than interpreting it yourself.

### What does the kitchen actually contain?

Describe the equipment the chef will have permission to use, not simply the appliances visible in a photograph. Note anything unavailable, faulty or reserved for another purpose.

Include fridge and freezer space, containers, cookware and the location of everyday ingredients. Ask who supplies missing items before the visit. A preference for batch cooking needs a practical conversation about storage as well as menu choices.

For Dubai apartments and villas, confirm the relevant building or community access arrangements. Identify the person responsible for checking visitor entry, parking and any delivery instructions; do not assume every property follows the same process.

## Who should approve menus and household changes?

**Give the chef one named day-to-day contact and define that person’s authority.** A personal assistant can coordinate decisions without becoming responsible for interpreting dietary instructions or approving spending beyond the household’s limits.

Use a simple responsibility table before cooking begins:

| Decision | Suggested decision owner | What to confirm |
|---|---|---|
| Household preferences | Household decision-maker | Which instructions are fixed and which allow flexibility |
| Weekly menu | Named approver | Whether approval is needed before ingredients are purchased |
| Ingredient purchases | Authorised budget holder | Spending boundaries and receipt requirements |
| Entry and kitchen access | PA or household contact | Who resolves an access problem on the day |
| Dietary changes | Household decision-maker | Who supplies and confirms the updated instruction |
| Changes to the service | Booking contact and provider | Whether the revised request has been accepted |

These are suggested responsibilities, not myCHEF booking terms. Agree the actual arrangement with the service provider and the household.

Name a backup contact for times when the main approver cannot respond. Explain which decisions should wait rather than leaving the chef to guess what silence means.

## How should the PA manage groceries, substitutions and spending?

Set out who buys ingredients, who checks existing supplies and who approves purchases. Treat these as separate tasks: an ingredient can be in the kitchen but unavailable for the chef’s use.

Before shopping, share a current inventory of relevant ingredients and ask whether the planned menu requires anything else. Mark items reserved for other household use. Avoid assuming pantry restocking is included in a cooking arrangement.

Agree a substitution process that distinguishes preference changes from dietary requirements. Replacing one vegetable is a different decision from changing an ingredient connected to an allergy or religious restriction.

Useful questions include:

- Who approves a purchase outside the agreed shopping list?
- What should happen when a requested ingredient cannot be sourced?
- Who receives receipts and records household purchases?
- Which items must never be substituted without explicit approval?
- Who owns unused ingredients and where should they be stored?

Keep spending authority separate from service scope. Permission to buy ingredients does not automatically authorise extra cooking, additional staff or a longer assignment.

## Why does a household chef brief vary between homes?

The useful level of detail depends on the work being requested. Focus on the factors that change what the chef needs to prepare or confirm:

- **Meal purpose:** Food served immediately needs a different handover from meals prepared for later.
- **Diner requirements:** Different dietary instructions or preferences need clear allocation by person.
- **Kitchen facilities:** Equipment and storage determine what needs discussion before menu approval.
- **Household routine:** School runs, working hours and other kitchen users affect practical access.
- **Purchasing arrangements:** Household-supplied ingredients require a different coordination process from chef-managed shopping.
- **Service boundaries:** Cooking, serving, clearing up and ingredient purchasing should be confirmed individually.

**myCHEF’s household chef service suits Dubai households seeking vetted chefs for home-cooked meals and weekly meal prep.** The PA should still confirm the scope of the particular booking; the service description does not settle every kitchen task or household request.

## Can you use a simple household chef brief template?

Yes. Use the following as a suggested template, removing fields that do not apply. Complete it with the household’s approved instructions rather than forwarding an unfinished form as though everything has been agreed.

### Household brief

- **Service required:** Meals for immediate eating, meal preparation, or a combination to discuss.
- **Household contact:** Main approver, PA and backup contact, with their responsibilities.
- **Diners:** Who is eating and which meals each person needs.
- **Dietary requirements:** Separate allergies, intolerances, religious requirements and preferences.
- **Menu preferences:** Favoured dishes, ingredients to avoid and acceptable repetition.
- **Kitchen arrangements:** Equipment, storage, containers and other kitchen users.
- **Purchasing:** Shopping responsibility, spending authority and receipt handling.
- **Access:** Address, entry process and contact for access problems.
- **Service boundaries:** Tasks to confirm, including serving and clearing up.
- **Handover:** Where meals go and how instructions and questions are communicated.

### Visit update

Confirm the cooking date, arrival arrangements, diners and approved menu. Add ingredients already available, changes since the previous visit and any questions requiring an answer before cooking starts.

End the update with the name of the approver. **Keep outstanding questions visible instead of hiding them inside a long message.**

## What should happen after the first cooking visit?

Ask for specific feedback rather than whether everything was “good”. Review portion suitability, seasoning, menu repetition, kitchen workflow and the usefulness of the handover.

Separate a permanent preference from a one-off request. If the household wants less chilli in future meals, update the standing brief; if a diner is away for the next visit, change only the visit update.

Confirm how meals intended for later use will be identified and how storage or reheating instructions will be supplied. Do not invent a general shelf life for every dish. Ask for instructions appropriate to the food prepared.

Keep feedback factual and actionable. “Please serve the sauce separately” gives a clearer instruction than “make it more family-friendly”.

## FAQ


**What should I send a household chef before the first visit?**

Send the diners, meals required, dietary instructions, kitchen arrangements, access details and approval contacts. Ask the chef or service coordinator to confirm any unresolved points before the visit.

**Can a personal assistant approve the weekly menu?**

A personal assistant can approve the weekly menu when the household has authorised that responsibility. Define whether that authority also covers substitutions, ingredient purchases and changes to the cooking request.

**Should allergies and dislikes go in the same list?**

No. Record allergies and intolerances separately from preferences, and identify the affected diner. Ask the chef to confirm whether the requirements can be accommodated in the household kitchen.

**Does a household chef bring groceries and equipment?**

Confirm groceries and equipment directly with the provider before the visit. Record who shops, which equipment is supplied and what the household needs to provide.

**How do I tell the chef about changes to the family schedule?**

Send a clearly marked visit update stating the revised diners, meals or access arrangements. Ask for confirmation when the change affects the agreed service.

**Does myCHEF provide chefs for recurring household cooking?**

myCHEF provides vetted chefs for home-cooked meals and weekly meal prep in Dubai. Share the household requirements and ask the team to confirm the proposed service scope.

**Should a family celebration use the regular household brief?**

A celebration needs a separate private dining or catering brief. Share the occasion, guest count, menu expectations and service required rather than assuming it falls within routine household cooking.

- [Do private chefs bring groceries and equipment?](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/do-private-chefs-in-dubai-bring-their-own-groceries-and-equipment)
- [Do private chefs clean the kitchen after cooking?](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/do-private-chefs-in-dubai-clean-the-kitchen-after-cooking)

## Make the next handover clear

The final line of the brief should explain what to do when instructions conflict. Name the person who resolves the question, and identify which decisions require confirmation before proceeding.

To discuss household cooking with myCHEF, send your preferred date or recurring schedule, Dubai location, diner or guest count and the service required. Include the dietary requirements and kitchen arrangements so the conversation starts with a useful brief.
